extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and advanced students of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for when a scientific principle, natural law, or property of matter is patentable only as applied (not in the abstract), and related requirements for specification, claim scope, and infringement. Focuses on English cases (Neilson, Hartley, Forsyth, Hall) illustrating enablement, claim breadth, and application vs principle distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for a mere principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a law, truth, or fact in nature, or an abstract principle, is not of itself a manufacture and cannot be the subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly stated by the judges: 'there can be no patent for a mere principle.' Stating a principle in a patent is not an invention unless connected to a practical application; the mere promulgation of a principle does not appropriate it to the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable when principle is embodied and connected with corporeal substances
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle that is 'so far embodied and connected with corporeal substances as to be in a condition to act, and to produce effects in any art, trade, mystery, or manual occupation' may be the subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the principle is presented as a practical manner of doing something — i.e., embodied in a machine or material means that produces an effect — it ceases to be an abstract principle and can be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable: new application of a natural agent with described mechanical means
rubrics_metrics.description: A new application of one of the forces of nature or properties of matter to produce a particular mechanical effect, accompanied by some described mechanical means of producing that effect, can be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Forsyth (detonating powder with a mechanical priming contrivance), Hall (use of gas flame to singe lace). The application must be described sufficiently to show how the agent is put to practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must disclose sufficient directions (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose by sufficient and clear directions some practical means by which persons of competent skill in the art can apply the principle and produce the effect contemplated by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baron Parke in Neilson directed the jury to inquire whether a person of ordinary skill could construct an apparatus from the specification to produce some beneficial effect; if so, the patent was valid for that claim. Enablement is a factual inquiry for skilled artisans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad/generic claim to a mode of applying a principle is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may claim the mode of carrying a principle into effect generally, without confining the claim to a single form of apparatus, provided some mode of carrying it into effect is disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Campbell: generality of claim 'is no objection whatever to the patent.' The ability to claim all modes of applying the principle, where the specification shows the principle applied to a special purpose, is seen as the merit of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: A patent for an application can extend to other modes of applying the same principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the patentee has discovered and described some mode of applying the principle to a practical result, he is entitled to protection against other modes that carry the same principle into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court treats use of different machinery to effect the same practical application as 'piracy of your original invention' and protects the patentee from other modes applying the same principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement may occur by differently constructed apparatus if it performs same practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of machinery or apparatus differing from that described in the specification may still infringe if it effects a practical application of the same principle embodied by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson: defendants' conduit-pipe system infringed the patent even though different in construction, because it heated the air intermediately and applied the same principle to furnaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent for a 'manufacture' requires material parts and an enabling description
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a manufacture (machine) should describe material parts composed so as to produce the described effect and be so described as to enable mechanics to put it in operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Kenyon held that a patent for an engine was for a manufacture because it was an engine 'composed of material parts, which were to produce the effect described, and the mode of producing which was so described as to enable mechanics to put it in operation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: New mode of building or method can be a manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: A new mode of building houses or ships to achieve a particular effect (e.g., preventing combustion) satisfies the statute as a 'manufacture' and is patentable as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hartley's patent for securing buildings/ships against fire (application of plates and wire, overlapping, fastening) was treated as a patent for a new mode of building — i.e., a manufacture — rather than an abstract discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of known elements yielding a new beneficial effect is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of known devices or steps (e.g., a blast and an exhaust) that together produce a new and beneficial result may be the subject of a valid patent even if individual elements were known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bovil v. Keyworth: combining an exhaust with a blast to carry off dusty air and improve flour was held patentable; the novelty was in the combination and its beneficial manufacturing effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality in specification is not fatal if it does not mislead skilled persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification's broad statements (e.g., that form or shape is 'immaterial') are permissible if a person of ordinary skill would not be misled and can, from the disclosure, construct an operative embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Neilson the jury found competent workmen would not be misled by the statement that form and size were immaterial; however, incorrect or misleading statements about essential matters can be problematic and were assessed by the court/jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee need not invent the natural agent itself to obtain protection
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor does not need to have invented the natural agent (e.g., heated air) — protection may attach to the inventor's novel application and the mechanical means for applying that agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson did not invent heated air, but his discovery and description of heating the blast and introducing it into the furnace, together with directions for an apparatus, sufficed to found patent protection for the application.
